title: Hard-Boiled Eggs
subject: Science
source: NYSED 2026 Grade 8 ILS Released Items, Questions 39-43
directions: Base your answers to questions 39 through 43 on the information below and on your knowledge of science.

intro.html: A student wanted to enter the New York State Fair 4-H Egg Preparation Demonstration Contest. The student researched the best way to prepare hard-boiled eggs. The student practiced various ways of hard-boiling eggs in the time limit allowed during the contest.

The student used four uncooked eggs, but dropped and cracked one on the kitchen counter while putting the other three eggs in a pot of room temperature water. The student used a stove to boil the water and cook the eggs. After cooking the three eggs, the eggs were taken out of the pot, allowed to cool, and the shells were removed. The eggs were then cut in half.

intro.caption: Model of Boiling Water and Eggs
intro.alt: Three drawings of the same pot with arrows between them. In the first drawing the pot holds water, and the pot and the water level are labeled. In the second drawing the water is full of bubbles and three eggs sit in it; the bubbles and the eggs are labeled. In the third drawing bubbles rise from the bottom of the pot and water vapor rises above it; the water vapor, the water level, and the bubbles are labeled.

cooktime.html: The cooking time for an egg (time required to raise the temperature from 21°C to 65°C in boiling water) depends on the properties of the egg. The graph below shows the effect of one property of an egg on this cooking time.

cooktime.caption: Relationship between Egg Cooking Time and Egg Mass
cooktime.alt: Line graph. The horizontal axis is Egg Mass in grams, labeled from 40 to 90. The vertical axis is Egg Cooking Time in minutes, labeled from 1 to 6. A single smooth line starts at about 2.4 minutes at the left edge of the graph and rises gradually to about 5.3 minutes at the right edge.

masses.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a plate with pieces of eggshell at the upper left, two hard-boiled egg halves cut open in the center, part of another cut egg at the right edge, and a whole egg at the lower right. Labels with lines point to the Shell, the Egg white, and the Yolk.

elevation.html: The environment can also affect the time needed to hard-boil an egg. The student practiced for the competition at their home in Caroga Lake, New York. The New York State Fair takes place near Onondaga Lake.
The graphs below represent some information about the temperature of boiling water and extra time required to hard-boil an uncooked egg at different elevations.

items.stem: The diagrams below represent the position and movement of particles of water in three different phases. Place the letters of the correct particle phase diagrams, from the choices below, into the correct boxes to complete the model of heating water used to hard-boil the eggs. The numbers 1 and 2 indicate different periods of time during which the water is heated.

parts.label: Select either Time Period 1 or Time Period 2 to indicate when each change in water took place. [1]

items.adapted: No wording change. On paper, students write the letter of a diagram on the line in each dashed box. On screen, they drag the diagram, labeled with its letter, into each box, as the exemplary response shows. A choice may be used in both boxes, as a letter may be written twice on paper. The printed "Letter:" prompt stays in the cropped figure as printed and is covered when a diagram is placed. The two parts are one 1-credit question, and both must be correct for credit.

items.stem: The student made a claim that a chemical change occurred while the eggs were boiled. Analyze the given information and identify the evidence that supports this claim. [1]
rubric: Credit: The provided evidence indicates a color change and production of a solid (when heated). This response is complete and correct. Sample responses: “The clear liquid egg turning into a white solid could be a possible chemical reaction.” / “A chemical change was made while the eggs were boiling. The color of the egg turned from clear to white, and the yolk turned from yellow liquid to yellow solid.”

Credit: Color change is identified, but because not all parts of the egg changed color and no part of the egg is specified, this portion of the response was not enough for credit. However, the provided evidence indicates the production of a solid (when heated). This response is sufficient for credit. Sample response: “the color of the egg changed and the inside went from a liquid to a solid”

No credit: Because nearly all of the observations from the table are provided, it is not possible to know which is being provided as evidence of chemical change. This response is insufficient for credit due to lack of specific evidence.

No credit: The physical change of the shell breaking is incorrectly provided as evidence of chemical change, and the discussion of chemical change does not include evidence from the table. This response is insufficient for credit due to lack of evidence.
No credit: While the response indicates that a new substance was made, no evidence from the table is provided. This response is insufficient for credit due to lack of evidence.
items.exemplar:
The clear, thick liquid of the egg turned white.
OR
The soft, yellow yolk became a solid and will not go back to an uncooked egg.
OR other valid response

items.stem: Which statement is supported by evidence in the graph?
options: A greater amount of time is needed to transfer more energy to cook an egg with more mass.
Eggs with more mass require less time and less energy to be transferred in order to be cooked.
The phase of the egg affects the egg’s mass and the amount of cooking time and energy transferred to the egg.
Time needed increases for eggs with more mass because less energy needs to be transferred to cook the egg.

items.stem: Which claim is supported by the evidence in the table?
options: As the egg is hard-boiled, the mass of the egg white increases as the mass of the egg shell decreases.
The mass of the egg is conserved as the egg is hard-boiled because the mass of the yolk increases as the mass of the egg white decreases.
The total mass of the egg increases as the egg boils because water gets trapped in the egg shell.
The total mass of the egg is conserved when the egg is cooked and becomes hard-boiled.
